lesson.title: The Truman Doctrine: America's Pledge to Contain Communism
lesson.summary: In March 1947 President Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey and declared that the United States would support free peoples resisting communist takeover anywhere in the world, marking the first concrete application of containment.
lesson.body:
Containment was a theory; the Truman Doctrine turned it into policy. In early 1947 Greece was locked in a civil war between its government and communist led guerrillas, while the Soviet Union was pressuring Turkey for control over the straits connecting the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. Britain had traditionally supported both countries, but a nearly bankrupt Britain, still recovering from the war, informed the United States in February 1947 that it could no longer afford to help. Truman's advisors saw a dangerous gap opening that the Soviets might fill.

On March 12, 1947, Truman addressed a joint session of Congress and asked for four hundred million dollars in military and economic aid for Greece and Turkey. More important than the money was the principle Truman announced, which became known as the Truman Doctrine: "It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures." Although Truman framed the request narrowly around Greece and Turkey, the language he used was sweeping, committing the United States, at least in principle, to opposing communist expansion anywhere in the world.

Congress approved the aid, and Greece's government eventually defeated the communist insurgency, while Turkey remained outside Soviet control. More significantly, the Truman Doctrine marked a permanent break with America's historic reluctance to make peacetime commitments outside the Western Hemisphere. It set the pattern that would repeat throughout the Cold War: the United States framing local conflicts around the world as tests of the broader struggle against communism, and using aid, and later troops, to prevent countries from falling into the Soviet orbit.
